bug_semantics: The unauthenticated /cgi-bin/api.values.get handler in the Grandstream GXP1600 firmware's 32-bit ARM /app/bin/gs_web binary parses the attacker-controlled request parameter as colon-delimited identifiers and copies each non-colon byte into a 64-byte stack buffer without checking the identifier length. An identifier longer than 63 bytes writes beyond that buffer, and repeated colon-delimited identifiers let an attacker place multiple terminating NUL bytes, overwrite saved registers including PC, build a ROP chain, and invoke system() as root.
flaw_origin: The flawed bounds-free identifier-copy loop belongs to Grandstream's proprietary GXP1600 firmware, not rapid7/metasploit-framework. Its source and version-control history are not public, so the exact introducing source commit is beyond the public-history boundary. Metasploit commit 08efa9cd16f254bfc8f2f4cee0550f3a851e0aa5 merely added an exploit for the already-existing device flaw after fixed firmware 1.0.7.81 had been released; it did not write the vulnerable /app/bin/gs_web code.
ai_marker: unavailable: there is no public BIC commit object for Grandstream's proprietary /app/bin/gs_web source, so BIC author, committer, bot identity, Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, and other trailer checks cannot be performed; no AI conclusion is drawn from the later Metasploit exploit commit
evidence: Rapid7's first-party disclosure (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ve-cve-2026-2329-critical-unauthenticated-stack-buffer-overflow-in-grandstream-gxp1600-voip-phones-fixed) identifies the vulnerable component as the native 32-bit ARM /app/bin/gs_web firmware binary and decompiles its api.values.get handler: attacker-controlled request_buffer bytes are appended to small_buffer[64] while part_length is incremented without a bound check. It documents PC control and the repeated-colon/NUL technique used to construct a ROP chain and execute commands as root.

The disclosure tested vulnerable firmware 1.0.7.79 and says users must upgrade to 1.0.7.81 or above. Its timeline records that Grandstream made 1.0.7.81 available, reaffirmed the issue resolved in that release, and that Rapid7 independently verified remediation by reverse engineering the public firmware. This is binary verification, not a public source commit.

Grandstream's release notes (https://firmware.grandstream.com/Release_Note_GXP16xx_1.0.7.81.pdf) list 1.0.7.81 for all six affected models, date it 2026-01-30, and include 'Fixed some security vulnerabilities.' The preceding 1.0.7.80 is dated 2025-12-31. The Metasploit module's description at modules/exploits/linux/http/grandstream_gxp1600_unauth_rce.rb:19-23 states that every firmware version below 1.0.7.81 is affected, and its check at lines 105-117 classifies version < 1.0.7.81 as vulnerable and 1.0.7.81 or later as safe.
NVD's analyzed CVE-2026-2329 record identifies the affected products as Grandstream GXP1610/GXP1615/GXP1620/GXP1625/GXP1628/GXP1630 firmware and CWE-121, not Metasploit Framework.

Repository search for api.values.get, small_buffer, sub_144B4, and gs_web finds only the exploit module, its documentation, and generated module metadata; the target firmware handler source is absent from the validated rapid7/metasploit-framework clone.

numactl-prefixed git log --follow for modules/exploits/linux/http/grandstream_gxp1600_unauth_rce.rb shows its first repository commit is 08efa9cd16f254bfc8f2f4cee0550f3a851e0aa5 (2026-02-17, 'add in the Grandstream modules'), whose parent is c0f73038f3fb4f76b4ed8a0c661be35639a9d1fc. git show --stat shows that commit adding Metasploit exploit/post modules and documentation; git cat-file confirms the exploit file is absent from that parent. This parent-tree result applies only to the exploit client and cannot establish absence of the firmware flaw.

The Metasploit addition postdates the vendor's 2026-01-30 fixed-firmware release and sends the crafted request to the phone; therefore it cannot be the BIC or direct fix for the earlier Grandstream firmware vulnerability. The advisory's GitHub PR reference is an exploit/VDB artifact, not the vulnerable product's patch history.
reasoning: The lifecycle is: an unknown, non-public Grandstream source revision first introduced an unchecked copy into a fixed 64-byte stack buffer in the unauthenticated api.values.get handler; the flaw persisted through at least firmware 1.0.7.80, was demonstrated on 1.0.7.79, and was removed in firmware 1.0.7.81. Rapid7 disclosed the issue after reverse-engineering both vulnerable and fixed firmware and then added a Metasploit exploit. Following the smallest-real-BIC rule, 08efa9cd16f254bfc8f2f4cee0550f3a851e0aa5 is rejected because it contains only attacker-side exploit/support code, was created after the vendor fix, and never wrote the vulnerable gs_web loop. The actual BIC, its immediate parent, and the actual fixing commit live in unavailable Grandstream source history; consequently immediate-parent absence, squash decomposition, commit SHA attribution, and BIC-only AI markers cannot be verified. This is a genuine public-history boundary, so BLOCKED is more accurate than NOT_AI or EVIDENCE_GAP.
remaining_gap: Grandstream's source repository and commit history for /app/bin/gs_web are not public. The missing artifacts are the source commit that first added the unbounded small_buffer copy, that commit's immediate parent tree, and the source commit that produced fixed firmware 1.0.7.81; without those commit objects, a BIC SHA, parent-absence proof, fix SHA, squash decomposition, and BIC-only AI attribution are impossible.
